extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, IP lawyers, judges, and law students
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating whether claimed inventions satisfy 35 U.S.C. § 101 (patentable subject matter), including application of Supreme Court precedents (Benson, Flook, Diehr) and tests like the machine-or-transformation inquiry. Focuses on business-methods, abstract ideas, and Information Age technologies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory categories of patentable subject matter (§101)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 101 specifies four independent categories of inventions or discoveries that are eligible for protection: processes, machines, manufactures, and compositions of matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 101 is an expansive, dynamic provision designed to encompass new and unforeseen inventions; its terms are broad but subject to the conditions and requirements of the Patent Act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Established exceptions to §101
rubrics_metrics.description: The Court's precedents provide three specific exceptions to §101's broad patent-eligibility principles: 'laws of nature, physical phenomena, and abstract ideas.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These exceptions are grounded in stare decisis and the policy that certain fundamental concepts are part of the public storehouse of knowledge and cannot be patented.

rubrics_metrics.name: §101 is a threshold test; satisfy other statutory requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: The §101 patent-eligibility inquiry is only a threshold test. Even if an invention qualifies under §101, it must also satisfy the conditions and requirements of this title, including novelty (§102), nonobviousness (§103), and full and particular description (§112).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants should not assume §101 eligibility guarantees a patent; novelty, nonobviousness, and adequate disclosure remain essential safeguards and may limit overbroad claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'process' (§100(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 100(b) defines 'process' as 'process, art or method, and includes a new use of a known process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter, or material.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statutory definition is somewhat circular; courts must interpret 'process' in light of precedent and context rather than only ordinary-language meaning. Whether 'method' includes business methods is not resolved textually alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine-or-transformation test (useful clue, not exclusive)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Federal Circuit formulation, a process is patent-eligible if (1) it is tied to a particular machine or apparatus, or (2) it transforms a particular article into a different state or thing. The Supreme Court held the machine-or-transformation test is a 'useful and important clue' but not the sole test for §101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat satisfaction (or failure) of the machine-or-transformation test as dispositive in all cases; it remains a strong investigative tool, especially for Industrial-Age technologies, but should not categorically exclude other modern inventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Business methods are not categorically excluded
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 101 does not categorically exclude business methods from being 'processes'; the term 'method' may include some methods of doing business. Federal statute (§273) contemplates the existence of at least some business method patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although business methods are not per se unpatentable, courts should be wary: business-method claims raise issues of vagueness and potential overbreadth, and other statutory requirements (§102/§103/§112) and precedent (e.g., abstract-idea doctrine) will constrain patentability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract-idea preemption bar
rubrics_metrics.description: An attempt to patent an abstract idea (e.g., a fundamental economic practice like hedging) is impermissible because it would preempt use of the idea in all fields and effectively grant a monopoly over the abstract idea itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims should be examined for whether they 'claim' the abstract idea in a way that preempts all practical applications; mere recitation of an abstract concept reduced to steps or a formula is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-solution activity/insignificant postsolution components
rubrics_metrics.description: Adding conventional or obvious post-solution activity cannot transform an unpatentable principle (e.g., a mathematical algorithm) into a patentable process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an application relies primarily on an abstract idea or mathematical formula, courts should assess whether any additional claimed steps are merely conventional or token post-solution components (Flook).

rubrics_metrics.name: Diehr principle — application of mathematical formulas/laws to a process may be patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: An application of a law of nature or mathematical formula to a known structure or process may be deserving of patent protection; the invention must be considered as a whole rather than dissecting old and new elements and ignoring the presence of old elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that integrate an algorithm or law into a concrete industrial process (e.g., molding rubber with computer calculations) can be patentable; evaluate the claim holistically and whether it is an attempt to patent the formula itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid categorical rules inconsistent with statutory text
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts should not read into the patent laws limitations and conditions that the legislature has not expressed; categorical exclusions (e.g., making the machine-or-transformation test exclusive) can be atextual and problematic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limitations on patentability should be rooted in precedent and statutory interpretation (including the established exceptions), not newly invented categorical rules that exceed the statute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special caution for Information-Age technologies
rubrics_metrics.description: The machine-or-transformation test may create uncertainty as to the patentability of software, advanced diagnostics, linear programming, data compression, and manipulation of digital signals—technologies typical of the Information Age.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because modern technologies often lack obvious machine-or-transformation characteristics, courts and examiners should apply §101 principles carefully to avoid improperly excluding novel innovations while guarding against overbroad patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy concern: set an appropriately high bar for business-method-like claims
rubrics_metrics.description: If a low bar is set for patenting business-method-like inventions, examiners and courts could be flooded with claims that chill creative endeavor and dynamic change; vagueness and suspect validity are particular problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use precedent (Benson, Flook, Diehr) and the requirements of novelty, nonobviousness, and particularity of description (§102/§103/§112) to limit grants and prevent undue preemption; consider statutory features like §273 and policy goals when assessing business-method claims.
